newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Blair set to avoid defeat on pensions.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Blair set to avoid defeat on pensions.

text.p: British opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair looked set on Wednesday to escape an embarrassing defeat over pensions policy that would have shattered the unity of his party's pre-election annual conference.

Blair, anxious to keep up the momentum of his party's drive for power after 17 years in opposition, appeared to have staved off demands for a budget-busting increase in state pensions sought by left-wingers.

The result of a vote on the controversial issue will not be published until Thursday, but backers of the pensions boost all but conceded defeat after several large unions, desperate for a Labour government, threw their weight behind Blair.

Social security spokeswoman Harriet Harman said voting for an increase in pensions estimated at 3.5 billion pounds ($5.5 billion) could cost Labour the next election, due by May, by reviving charges that it remains at heart a tax-and-spend party.
"We owe it to (pensioners) not to make promises we know we can't keep and that we know could threaten our chance to help them in government," Harman said.
Although delegates in their heads looked likely to follow Harman and Blair, their hearts were clearly with veteran left-winger Baroness Barbara Castle.
Castle, 85, set the conference alight with an impassioned appeal to restore the link between earnings growth and pensions for Britain's 10 million retirees.
A former Labour social security secretary, Castle showed that age had not dimmed her ability to hold an audience in her hands with a witty, withering speech that earned her two standing ovations.

"It's no good, comrades, saying we want pensioners to take their rightful share of growing national prosperity and then say we will not restore the very mechanisms designed to ensure that they can and will," she said.

The rapturous reception she received showed that there are still signs of life in the corpse of socialism in Britain -- despite Blair's modernisation drive that has dragged Labour to the political centre since he became leader two years ago.

A defeat on pensions would not have chained Blair to an expensive spending pledge, but it would have taken the gloss off the widely-acclaimed keynote speech he made on Tuesday promising to lead Britain into a new age of achievement.
Blair fired up his own party and stirred commentators on both the left and right of politics with a speech deeply personal in content and almost evangelical in tone.

Even the mass-selling Sun newspaper, which claimed to have won the last general election for the Conservatives in defiance of opinion poll forecasts, was moved to describe it as "the speech of his life", headlining its report "President Blair".

With polls giving Blair a lead of 20 points plus, and the government reeling from the latest press revelations about sleaze in the Conservative Party, Blair's path to victory has never seemed more assured.

But aides, remembering a triumphalist eve of poll rally in 1992 before Labour's unexpected loss, warned party supporters against celebrating too soon. Blair himself repeatedly stressed that victory had to be earned by winning the trust of voters.

"The heartfelt enthusiasm of the party delegates for the speech belied the central message for the electorate -- that Mr Blair by no means believes that the next election is in the bag," wrote the Independent's Tony Bevins. ($1=.6385 Pound)
